Most people in the region are pretty ignorant when it comes to firearm usage in their own country. Hell, if you go outside to the middle of the countryside on a Saturday in winter you'll hear gunfire all around you. Clay shooting as well as game (mainly partridge/pheasant) is extremely popular and the relatively high density of cities & towns here mean you are never very far from some sort of shooting related activities. To most people here the 'countryside' is just the green bit in between the cities. Their only real time in it is spent looking out of a car / train window, or flying over it in a plane on the way to a popular holiday destination. They neither know nor care about any of the activities that go on there.  ...and as someone who shoots I'm perfectly happy with this ignorance as it keeps away the "won't somebody think of the children" brigade. --- Hell there are three .50 cal ranges within a couple of hours drive of my house. Not even many yanks can say that.

Yeah, handguns are super-restricted. The only folk who can own handguns here are those who require one as part of their job. For civilian ownership other than police, your legitimate reason will normally be 'for the humane dispatch of distressed animals'; So we're talking vets, game wardens, etc. An acquaintance of mine has a fairly large sheep farm and owns one for this reason. It's a smooth-bore .38 special revolver with all but two of the chambers filled in. Which means it's wildly inaccurate at anything over a couple of feet, and only has a capacity for two shots. But as it's specifically for humane dispatch that's all you need.

So few crimes are committed with rifles (of any calibre) that it's not even a blip. --- We actually have no calibre restrictions here whatsoever (or restrictions on mag size limits). But you do need to show that you have access to land suitable for the calibre you wish to own. For instance, if I wanted to own a 30mm recoilless rifle it'd be fine so long as I can show I have permission somewhere suitable to use it. There are a few military ranges that allow civilians to use such calibres on their ranges, so as long as you're a member of a club that has access to such a range you're a'ok. Also, the region is far more permissive than most US states when it comes to silencers/suppressors (we call them moderators). Most shooting organizations and even most police forces recommend that they be attached to all rifles.   As far as we're concerned it's better for your hearing, less likely to spook your quarry, causes less noise pollution, and as far as the police are concerned it causes far less false call outs. They aren't seen as "tools of assassins" here, which seems to be the case in the US. --- We do have strict restrictions on action types though.... Other than .22 rimfire all rifles have to be manually cycled. Which basically means no semi auto rifles (semi-auto & pump-action shotguns are fine though). That kinda sucks, but hey-ho; Such is life.

None of these issues are insurmountable. A basic action camera recording 1080p footage @30fps can manage around 2.5 hours of continuous recording. For a full 8 hour shift plus a bit in reserve you'd need an action camera type device with a battery four times the size. Current action camera batteries are quite small, so 4x the size still isn't beyond the realms of possibility. In any case, many sources claim that as much as 50% of an officer's time on shift is spent in the station filling out paperwork, so in that case the battery would only need to be twice the size not four times. --- As for getting the footage off the cameras that part is relatively straightforward. As soon as an officer places their camera on charge back at the station their camera would authenticate with the video server and automatically sync up the footage it's recorded since its last charge, along with which officer was using the camera at the time. When the officer fills in their activity report at the end of their shift the times of incidents the officer attended that day are sent to the video server which flags those periods of the officer's daily footage for long term storage. You'd probably want a system where officer logged incidents are stored for a few months or until required as evidence, with all daily footage kept for a week and deleted on a rolling basis as long as the officer has no complaints filed against them. Storage is cheap as shit nowadays anyway. Based on my own CCTV system 8 hours of continuous 1080 footage @30fps would come in at around 30GB. Meaning that assuming police work a 5-day week the rolling storage you'd need would be about 150GB of storage per officer (which currently costs £20/TB). ...You'd probably want to double the amount needed though to allow for backups of everything. The amount of long term storage needed would depend on how much of an officer's time is actually spent attending incidents, which I'd imagine isn't actually that high overall. --- So yeah, I don't see any part of this that is beyond technically possible. And the storage side at least shouldn't break the bank.

"Discipline" doesn't have to mean pain. I don't think your trainer understands this. While applying physical pain *can* work to condition a dog to do certain things, it has to be done correctly, and even when it is it can be deeply unhealthy for the relationship between you and the dog and can lead to a fear-based relationship rather than one of love and mutual respect. I'll readily admit that I use a small amount of discipline (as well as lots of fun and rewards) to train my dogs but only under extreme (life & death) circumstances would I consider using physical pain to reinforce a point. For example, a gentle short-sharp tug on a long training lead doesn't cause any actual pain and is a valid way of correcting a dog which is having issues with recall (along with praise & rewards when the dog does as its asked). Dragging the dog about by the lead/collar half-choking it however doesn't teach the dog anything and is just inflicting pain for the sake of it. --- As the dog's owner you don't need to constantly show physical "dominance", as that will eventually just cause the dog to fear & resent you (or worse, it'll say "fuck you" and just do the opposite of anything you say). As the 'pack leader' you do want the dog to respect you though (and it needs you to show it respect in return). You earn that respect by fulfilling the dogs needs in terms of food, shelter, love, affection, fun, sufficient exercise, and where needed... discipline.   The way I see it is if you fail to give enough of any one of those the dog will start to fail to see you as the leader and that's when you'll likely start to have behavioral problems.

Be pro-active in speaking to your neighbors. Explain that you've just got a new dog so there may be some period of separation anxiety noise to start with, but that you're aiming for them to get over it as soon as possible. Push home the point that you're aware of the noise your dog may be making and are actively working to correct it. Stuff that's worked for me with fixing separation anxiety (and things I've recommended to others and have heard positive results from).... * Put some of your dirty clothes in their cage/basket so they can smell you when you aren't around (don't use your best duds in case the dog chews them). * Leave a radio or TV on. Preferably with talking or some soothing music (not death metal). * Don't make a big deal about it when you leave, don't spend ages saying 'goodbye'. Quickly and quietly leave the house with the minimum of fuss and/or noise. * If using a cage put the dog in it a while before you leave so the dog isn't associating the cage with being left alone. * Don't give them any fuss when you return until they've calmed down. As hard as it is, ignore them completely if you have to. This pushes the idea that it's not them being hyper that has caused you to return and give them fuss, but them being calm. * If you leave the house and hear noise straight away, don't go back in to reassure them as you'll just be reinforcing that behavior. * To start with, only leave the dog alone straight after they've had a long walk & off-lead run and have burned off a load of energy. Assuming they can hold it, preferably wear them out *then* feed them so they also have a full stomach along with being tired out.
